source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC12502574 (title confirmed): Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Recommendations, Limitations, Conclusions, Appendix 1 (Table 1, all 35 rows, and the printed search strings) and the reference list read in full. Fig. 1 (PRISMA flow diagram, an image) not viewed. Primary studies not read.

claims.overstatement: Not supported as worded: (1) the opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines had a lower in-treatment death rate (1.31 against 1.79) than those without benzodiazepine prescribing only; the review gives no in-treatment rate for the briefly prescribed group in the text, and Table 1 says patients with occasional benzodiazepine prescriptions had the lowest in-treatment mortality, so 'than the others' is wrong for that group. (2) 'Most drug-checking sources tested how well laboratory methods detect benzodiazepines': by Table 1, 5 or 6 of the 11 evaluated detection (Borden, Gozdzialski, Laxton, Mullin [50], Laing, partly Tobias), mostly point-of-care or portable instruments checked against laboratory confirmation; the rest report what services found, behaviour after test strips (Park, Gelberg) or users' views (Reed). Say 'about half ... point-of-care and laboratory methods'. (3) In the magnitude, 'benzodiazepine-type drugs in 116 of 555 samples, 15 of them expected to be benzodiazepines': the 15 are of the 555; the review does not say how many of the 116 were among them. Understatement: the claim omits the one observational study with numbers on behaviour after drug checking (Gelberg et al., 541 adults: a positive test-strip result went with using less, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, a reduction in quantity used reported as 20-fold when benzodiazepines were tested, which the Results word causally), and omits that the authors themselves describe drug checking as having consistent positive outcomes; the 'insufficient' judgment is the editors' and is justified by the designs, but the authors' reading should be shown as theirs. Minor: 'most often together with opioids, stimulants or alcohol' is not quantified in the review; the isolation-hotel source (Brothers et al.) is a medRxiv preprint. No dosing or administration guidance in the claim (the review's '50% of usual dose' and 'up to 30 mg daily' are rightly omitted).
claims.note: Numbers checked against Table 1 and text: 35 sources; groups 11, 5, 9, 10; designs recounted from Table 1: 17 quantitative, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews (one a rapid review), 1 policy analysis, no randomized trial (the Results text's own breakdown, 20/1/4/2/1, adds to 28). 59 samples, 36%, 78%, 9%, 62%; 11 of 15; 33/139 = 23.7%; 2, 4 and 14 of 20; 116 and 15 of 555; 24 (41%); 68 of 103, 96% to 68%, 22% to 7%, 69%; 6 of 77; more than 70; 278, 127, 72/34/51 months, 1.31/1.79, 450% to 5.90 (5.90/1.31 = 4.50, an increase of 350%: editors' calculation reproduced); 4 of 5; 57 to 23 (-59.6%) and 160 to 238 (+48.8%), cited from reference 82, a two-page response letter (Lloyd et al., 2017); 89% (Kentucky, six clinics); 183/1112 = 16.5%; 6635/17,616 = 37.7%. Search rerun on 7 July 2025 confirmed. 'Presence, not cause' and 'involved' wording respected.

anchors.locator: Methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Method
anchors.extracted: PsycINFO, MEDLINE, Web of Science and Embase; first search 14 February to 30 March 2024; rerun 7 July 2025 with the same strategy (249 new unique records, 17 full texts, 7 added).

anchors.locator: Methods › Study selection criteria, paragraph after the inclusion criteria and last paragraph; Limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: No exclusion on study quality (scoping methodology); protocol registered on OSF as a systematic review and reframed as a scoping review because of heterogeneous designs and quality; no risk-of-bias assessment and no meta-analysis.

anchors.locator: Results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 2351 records, 1048 duplicates, 1303 screened, 88 full texts, 53 excluded, 35 included; themes direct interventions 16 (drug checking 11, agonist treatment 5), policy 9 (rescheduling 3, prescribing 3, toxicosurveillance 3), population-specific 10. The Results text gives designs as 20 quantitative, 1 qualitative, 4 reviews, 2 mixed, 1 policy analysis (sum 28).

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1, Study design column (all 35 rows)
anchors.extracted: Reader's recount: quantitative 17 (pilot, brief report, secondary analysis, retrospective cohort, retrospective analysis or case-note review, cross-sectional survey, implementation, unspecified), qualitative 9, mixed-methods 4, reviews 4 (including one rapid review), policy analysis 1; no randomized trial.

anchors.locator: Results › Direct interventions › Drug checking, 2nd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Gozdzialski et al.; Laxton et al.)
anchors.extracted: Portable GC-MS (59 samples): 62% of carfentanil-containing and 36% of etizolam-containing samples identified, 78% when etizolam was above 3% by weight; infrared spectroscopy 9% of etizolam-containing samples. Miniature PCSI-MS/MS quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples in which strips and/or FTIR failed to detect or quantify it.

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Tobias et al.)
anchors.extracted: Community drug checking, October 2017 to March 2020: of 139 samples expected to be Xanax, 33 (23.7%) contained alprazolam by FTIR; 88 of 122 (72.1%) positive on benzodiazepine strips; of 20 confirmed by GC-MS, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other actives, 14 (70%) other actives only.

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Scarfone et al.); Results › Drug checking, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Toronto, 555 samples: 15 expected to be benzodiazepines; benzodiazepine-type drugs confirmed in 116 samples (etizolam 95, flualprazolam 46); samples containing them were 41% (n = 24) of all samples associated with a negative effect (adverse health event, extreme sedation or overdose).

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Park et al.); Results › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Baltimore pilot, 103 female sex workers who use drugs; package of baseline survey, tailored messaging, five fentanyl test strips with training and a naloxone kit; 68 completed the one-month survey; 84% used a strip, 86% had a positive result, 69% did a harm-reduction behaviour after a result; pre-post: injection frequency 40% to 25%, benzodiazepine use 22% to 7%, solitary use 96% to 68%; no control group.

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Gelberg et al.); Results › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Multi-state community-based observational study, 541 adults, 28 days: a positive test-strip result was associated with using smaller amounts, taking turns and having naloxone nearby; four-fold reduction in quantity overall, 20-fold when benzodiazepines were tested, tenfold stimulants, twofold opioids; the Results text says the positive result 'resulted in' the reduction. Omitted by the claim.

anchors.locator: Results › Direct interventions › Agonist treatment, 1st paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Brothers et al.; O'Carroll et al.); reference 55
anchors.extracted: Isolation hotels: 77 residents, 62 took the safer-supply offer, 6 (8%) received prescribed benzodiazepines; low adverse events, no overdoses and high isolation completion for the programme as a whole (source is a 2022 medRxiv preprint). Dublin policy analysis: more than 70 people initiated on benzodiazepine maintenance; staff-reported benefits; no feedback from service users collected.

anchors.locator: Results › Policy › Prescribing, 2nd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Bakker and Streel)
anchors.extracted: Inner-London general practice case-note review, 278 OST patients: 127 on benzodiazepine maintenance retained 72 months against 34 (none) and 51 (brief); in-treatment mortality 1.31 per 100 patient-years against 1.79 without; post-treatment mortality rose 450% (to 5.90 per 100 years, Table 1) against 191% and 125%. Table 1 adds that patients with occasional prescriptions had the lowest in-treatment mortality.

anchors.locator: Results › Policy › Rescheduling, 1st paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Caulkins et al.)
anchors.extracted: 2021 review: five evaluations of Australia's 2014 move of alprazolam from Schedule 4 to 8; four reported large declines in alprazolam use; declines in prescribing, dispensing, overdose deaths and poison-centre calls described; 2017 restrictions no substantial effect; extent of substitution disputed.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Latent impacts of rescheduling, 1st paragraph; reference 82
anchors.extracted: Alprazolam-related deaths fell 60% (57 in 2012 to 23 in 2015) while benzodiazepine overdose deaths rose 49% (160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015); source is a two-page response letter (Lloyd et al., 2017); no definitions of the deaths; different start years.

anchors.locator: Results › Policy › Rescheduling, 2nd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Fountain et al.)
anchors.extracted: UK temazepam gel-capsule rescheduling, qualitative, 100 people with long-term polydrug use: fewer people injecting capsules, continued injection of tablets, higher prices, more acquisitive crime, substitution with flunitrazepam.

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Agrawal et al.; Syrjanen et al. [66]; Doyon et al.)
anchors.extracted: Kentucky, six clinics, 'no benzodiazepine' formulary from 2016: prescriptions down 89% over two years, caseloads not reduced. Victoria emergency departments 2020 to 2022: 183 of 1112 drug-toxicity presentations (16.5%) involved benzodiazepine-type NPS. Poison centre: 17,616 tablet-identification calls in 20 months, safety information to 6635 (37.7%); judged feasible, no outcome evaluation.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Conclusion; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors: drug checking the most widely reported approach 'with consistent positive outcomes across studies' (abstract), most prevalent and pragmatic; prescribing and policy mixed; notable absence of harm reduction for people not seeking abstinence or formal treatment; more robust evaluation needed.

claims.overstatement: Not supported as worded: 'The only numbers come from a before-and-after pilot' (statement) and 'No comparison and no effect estimate' (magnitude). The review also reports Gelberg et al. (541 adults who use drugs, 28 days, observational): after a positive fentanyl test-strip result people reported using smaller amounts, taking turns and having naloxone nearby, with the reduction in quantity used reported as four-fold overall and 20-fold when benzodiazepines were tested (Results › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph, in causal wording; Table 1, as an association). It compares behaviour after positive against negative results among people who test, not people who used a practice against people who did not, and its outcome is behaviour, not harm, so the claim's 'no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not' still stands. If added, it should be reported as an association with reported quantity, without amounts. Minor: '(45, interviewed)': the review gives a qualitative study of 45 but does not say interviews. The claim correctly leaves out the forum's dosing and frequency details, the 'tester shot' and 'smaller amount' examples and the end-of-day timing in the ethnography.
claims.note: Checked: flubromazolam forum (Andersson and Kjellgren, qualitative, N = 122 in Table 1) and the five practices named; British Columbia women and gender-diverse people (Speed et al., qualitative, 45); Melbourne ethnography (Dwyer, one participant); Bangkok survey of 252 (Kerr et al., education to avoid injecting alone); Baltimore pilot 68 of 103, 69%, 96% to 68%; Limitations (term-based search; peer-led resources not covered); Conclusions (absence for people not seeking abstinence or treatment). Borden et al. adds unquantified accounts ('several' samples returned for destruction; smaller doses, not using alone, carrying naloxone reported).

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Andersson and Kjellgren); Results › Population-specific approaches › Online drug forums, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Qualitative analysis of a Swedish forum (Flashback), N = 122: shared practices included restricting one's own access to the drug while using, staying at home, controlling frequency of use, deterring simultaneous alcohol use and comparing vendors and batches (and low doses, not reproduced). Accounts, not evaluated.

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Speed et al.); Results › Population-specific approaches › Women who use drugs
anchors.extracted: Qualitative study, 45 women and gender-diverse people who use drugs, British Columbia, COVID-19: benzodiazepine contamination and reduced service access raised overdose risk; risk of sexual assault noted; participants formed informal peer networks to check on one another.

anchors.locator: Results › Policy › Rescheduling, 3rd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Dwyer)
anchors.extracted: Melbourne street-based ethnography: one participant described using temazepam at home to reduce the risk of losing money or drugs or being arrested while less vigilant.

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Kerr et al.); Results › Population-specific approaches › People who inject benzodiazepines
anchors.extracted: Cross-sectional survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok; authors list four harm-reduction needs, including education to avoid injecting alone. Recommendation, not evaluated.

anchors.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Park et al.); Results › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: 103 enrolled, 68 followed up at one month; 69% did a harm-reduction behaviour after a result (for example asked someone to check on them); solitary use 96% to 68%; no control group.

anchors.locator: Results › Direct interventions › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Gelberg et al.)
anchors.extracted: 541 adults, 28 days, observational: positive test-strip results associated with smaller amounts used, taking turns and naloxone nearby; four-fold reduction in quantity overall, 20-fold for benzodiazepine tests. Numbers and a comparison (positive against negative results) beyond the pilot.

anchors.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Search hinged on the term harm reduction and may have missed studies; peer-led resources and peer-to-peer advice not covered; authors find harm-reduction interventions notably absent for people not seeking abstinence or formal treatment.

key_findings.correction: Arithmetic rechecked: rerun counts 230 + 482 + 444 + 1195 = 2351; first search 1850; 1303 - 249 = 1054, 88 - 17 = 71, 35 - 7 = 28.
Table 1 also gives a four-fold reduction in quantity overall for Gelberg et al.
Add: Table 1 says patients with occasional benzodiazepine prescriptions had the lowest in-treatment mortality; the 1.31 against 1.79 comparison is with patients not prescribed benzodiazepines only.
Reference 82 checked: a two-page response letter (Int J Drug Policy 2017;39:138-9).
The review gives Speed et al. as a qualitative study of 45; it does not say interviews.

reporting_issues.note: Text countries 8+8+4+2+2+4+1+1+1+2+3 = 36; Table 1 gives 35 with no Welsh source.
Also: 2351 - 218 - 127 = 2006, not 249, so the rerun's 249 can only be records new to the first search, which the text does not say.

Reference list checked: 32 is Rigoni et al. 2019 (Jakarta) and no other Rigoni entry exists; 63 is McBride et al. 1997 (amphetamine prescribing); Guina et al. is 64 in the list, 65 in Table 1; Bakker and Streel is 65.
Reference 18 is the ONS bulletin on deaths related to drug poisoning in England and Wales (2023 registrations); 10,964/1145 = 9.58; 902/1337 = 67.5%.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high, agreed; no included source is by the review's authors.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. The interpretation-gap text's 'most drug-checking sources test how well analytical methods detect benzodiazepines' is borderline: 5 or 6 of 11 by Table 1.

missed: The isolation-hotel source (Brothers et al., reference 55) is cited as a 2022 medRxiv preprint, so the agonist-treatment outcome for 6 of 77 residents rests on a non-peer-reviewed report.
Table 1 (Bakker and Streel) says the occasional-prescription group had the lowest in-treatment mortality, which qualifies the maintained group's 1.31 against 1.79.
